episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Friday, March 20, 2026. Here's what's happening in A.I. and higher education.
-
Today, academic libraries emerge as campus A.I. literacy hubs, while the Department of Labor invests millions in community college training.
-
In Insights and Trends today, academic libraries are evolving into what researchers call A.I. sandboxes, neutral spaces where students and faculty can experiment with tools responsibly.

According to Inside Higher Ed, Bryn Mawr College library is using a platform called BoodleBox that gives centralized access to multiple A.I. tools while prioritizing privacy. At West Point, librarians developed a custom curriculum-mapping chatbot. Carnegie Mellon and the University of Pennsylvania offer hands-on A.I. literacy workshops.

Lauren Dodd at Bryn Mawr stated that, quote, A.I. literacy is just a new dimension of information literacy, end quote. The skills librarians have been teaching, evaluating sources, understanding bias, thinking critically about information, apply directly to working with A.I. systems. BoodleBox now serves over 800,000 users across more than 1,300 campuses.
-
Turning to Practical Tips, the San Diego Community College District is hosting InnovAItion Day today, March 20.

According to SD City Times, the event brings together faculty, staff, and students to explore responsible A.I. use in education. Student-led panels will feature discussions about A.I.'s role in learning. The district is using the event as an opportunity for cross-campus conversation about A.I. policies and practices.
-
In Insights and Trends, a Jobs for the Future survey finds student A.I. use for education increased from 59 percent in 2024 to 70 percent in 2026.

According to Inside Higher Ed, 48 percent of students seek A.I. guidance from social media versus only 23 percent from educational institutions. This indicates students prefer informal learning channels despite institutional efforts to provide A.I. training. The gap between where students learn about A.I. and where institutions want them to learn highlights a communication challenge for higher education.
-
In Ethical A.I., the EU A.I. Act enters full effect for universities in August 2026.

According to The Education Magazine, the regulation classifies A.I.-assisted admissions systems and student performance analytics as high-risk. European universities must demonstrate compliance by August 2026 or face penalties. The regulation represents the most comprehensive A.I. governance framework affecting higher education globally.
-
Also in Insights and Trends, the U.S. Department of Labor is putting $65 million toward helping community colleges develop short-term training programs that qualify for Workforce Pell.

According to Inside Higher Ed, this sixth round of Strengthening Community College Training Grants will make around 10 awards ranging from $6.5 million to $10.8 million. Across previous rounds, 207 community colleges in 35 states received a combined $265 million, supporting sectors including advanced manufacturing, healthcare, IT, cybersecurity, and clean energy.
-
In Case Studies, Google.org awarded $2 million to the National Applied AI Consortium to expand applied A.I. training across the United States.

According to Insight Into Academia, NAAIC, anchored by Miami Dade College with Houston City College and Maricopa Community Colleges, has supported 320 colleges across 46 states, trained over 1,000 faculty, and reached 31,000 students in its first year. The consortium aims to train 10,000 faculty and reach one million students by 2027. Executive Director Antonio Delgado emphasized that community colleges can redefine who gets to participate in the A.I. economy.
-
That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
